paper_title: Improving and Expanding Video Editing Capabilities Without Videos

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Image editing models can follow a wide range of instructions, but video editing models still lag behind, limited in part by the difficulty of collecting paired source and edited videos. Is it possible to transfer advanced image editing capabilities to video editors without new paired videos? We introduce Image-to-Video Transfer (I2VT), which improves pretrained video editors and expands them to new editing tasks using an image editor. It enables efficient post-training with no architectural changes and no new videos, using only individual images. Our key idea is to let the video editor role-play as an image editor: it edits an image as a one-frame video, with the image editor guiding the video editor's predictions at each denoising step. Although the video editor sees only single images during training, at test time it applies the improved and expanded capabilities to whole video clips while preserving temporal consistency. To push the boundaries of video editing, we introduce OpenVE++, an extension of OpenVE-Bench that adds four new editing tasks useful for video production, including action changes, expression changes, body movements, and scene relighting. Our experiments across three different video editors show that I2VT improves existing editing capabilities and expands them to new tasks, and our models achieve state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on both OpenVE-Bench and OpenVE++.

sections.content: Image editing models can follow wide range of instructions, but video editing models still lag behind, limited in part by the difficulty of collecting paired source and edited videos. Is it possible to transfer advanced image editing capabilities to video editors without new paired videos? We introduce Image-to-Video Transfer (I2VT), which improves pretrained video editors and expands them to new editing tasks using an image editor. It enables efficient post-training with no architectural changes and no new videos, using only individual images. Our key idea is to let the video editor role-play as an image editor: it edits an image as one-frame video, with the image editor guiding the video editors predictions at each denoising step. Although the video editor sees only single images during training, at test time it applies the improved and expanded capabilities to whole video clips while preserving temporal consistency. To push the boundaries of video editing, we introduce OpenVE++, an extension of OpenVE-Bench that adds four new editing tasks useful for video production, including action changes, expression changes, body movements, and scene relighting. Our experiments across three different video editors show that I2VT improves existing editing capabilities and expands them to new tasks, and our models achieve state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on both OpenVE-Bench and OpenVE++. 1 Figure 2. Motivation and intuition. Left: image editors handle complex edits such as actions and relighting on single frames, whereas video editors lack the paired data to learn them. Our goal is video editor that makes these edits while keeping the video temporally consistent. Middle: can video editor learn to edit images by treating each image as one-frame video? Right: video editing ability improves while temporal quality remains comparable. 1. Introduction Recent image editing models have advanced rapidly and can follow detailed instructions and offer fine-grained control over wide range of edits [4, 5, 8, 17, 58, 68, 73, 89, 110]. This progress has been supported by increasingly diverse image editing datasets [6, 87, 103, 106, 111]. However, current video editors [2, 13, 24, 28, 93, 116] still perform only moderately well on basic edit types such as object removal. They struggle even more with edits that change persons actions, facial expressions, body movements, or scenes lighting, although video production often needs these edits [7, 18, 63, 107, 115] (Figure 2, left). This gap remains even though modern image and video editors are built in similar ways: they use the same flowmatching objective and similar diffusion transformer (DiT) architectures [64], and many recent models also share variational autoencoder (VAE) [37] latent space [77, 79, 89, 100]. One reason video editors still lag behind is training data. good training pair for video editing must include an edited video that follows the instruction closely over the whole clip while leaving unrelated regions unchanged. Yet current data pipelines struggle to produce such videos, especially when edits become complex and diverse [2, 7, 62]. This raises question: can video editor improve its existing editing capabilities and expand them to new tasks without new paired videos? To answer this question, we introduce Image-to-Video Transfer (I2VT), which efficiently improves and expands pretrained video editor using only images instead of new paired videos. Our intuition is that an image is simply oneframe video, so editing images well could be foundation for editing videos well. We therefore let the video editor role-play as an image editor: it edits source image as one-frame video under the supervision of frozen image editor. direct way to give this supervision is offline distillation, which fine-tunes the video editor on the image editors pre-computed edit results. I2VT instead lets the image editor tell the video editor how to update its current noisy prediction at each step of its own denoising trajectory (Figure 3). Although the video editor sees only single images during training, at test time it applies the improved and expanded capabilities to whole video clips while preserving temporal consistency (Figure 1). To push the boundaries of video editing, we introduce OpenVE++, an extension of OpenVE-Bench [24] that adds four editing tasks useful for video production: Action Change, Expression Change, Body Movement, and Scene Relighting (Figure 4). These tasks test whether video editors can change persons performance and scenes lighting, which video production often requires [7, 63, 115]. Across three video editors, our experiments show that I2VT improves basic edits and enables new tasks that their pretrained base editors barely perform, and the resulting models achieve state-of-the-art (SOTA) results among the open-source video editors we compare. Our contributions are as follows: We propose I2VT, which improves and expands pretrained video editors by letting them role-play as image editors, without new paired videos or architecture changes. We introduce OpenVE++, an extension of OpenVEBench that adds four new editing tasks useful for video production: action changes, expression changes, body movements, and scene relighting. We validate I2VT across three video editing models: editing capabilities improved and expanded with single images generalize to whole video clips while preserving temporal consistency, and the resulting models achieve SOTA results on OpenVE-Bench and OpenVE++. 2. Method Image-to-Video Transfer (I2VT) lets pretrained video editor role-play as an image editor: it edits an individual image as one-frame video, with frozen image editor guiding its predictions at each denoising step. During fine-tuning, the video student takes one source image and an editing instruction at time. I2VT matches the teachers velocity predictions on the students own denoising trajectory. Task and Training Data We build I2VT-17K by sampling individual frames from OpenVE-3M [24], dataset already commonly used to train video editors [49, 108]. We organize these images and their instructions into two pools: the OpenVE pool for basic edits and the OpenVE++ pool for four new task groups. Action Change covers head, gaze, and arm edits where the person stays in place, distinct from Body Movement, which involves whole-person movements like crouching, jumping, sitting down, standing up, and turning (Figure 4). Expression Change covers facial expressions such as sadness, happiness, and anger, and Scene Relighting changes the light type and direction. For the new tasks, Vision-Language Model (VLM) describes the source frame so that we can choose suitable edit and write its instruction. We accept an instruction only if the frame contains what the edit needs and does not already show the requested change, so raising an arm, for example, requires that arm to be visible and not already raised. The two instructions specify the same edit, with wording adapted to each model: cimg refers to single image, while cvideo refers to video and may include temporal requirements such as throughout the video. This conversion can be automated with simple text replacements. 3. Effectiveness of I2VT We apply our approach to three pretrained video editors and study three research questions: Can I2VT strengthen basic editing capabilities (Section 3.3)? Can I2VT teach video editors new editing tasks using only images (Section 3.4)? How does online distillation compare with offline distillation (Section 3.5)? 3.1. Experimental Setup Models and Data. We evaluate I2VT on Bernini-R1.3B [79], Bernini-R-14B, and VideoCoF [100], using the powerful image editor JoyAI-Image-Edit [77] as their shared teacher. The teacher and students share the 16-channel Wan 2.1 VAE latent representation [80], and their detailed architecture descriptions are in the appendix. Training Configuration. We fine-tune each base editor for 200 steps with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) [27], where each I2VT update uses = 10 rollout steps per image and global batch size of 24, or 48 when training jointly on both pools. Evaluation Benchmarks and Metrics types. OpenVE++ Benchmark. Existing video editing benchInspired by marks mainly evaluate basic edit ImgEdit-Bench [102] and GEdit-Bench [53], we introduce OpenVE++, which extends OpenVE-Bench with four new categories defined in Section 2.4. OpenVE++ comprises 207 videoinstruction pairs across four categories (4273 per category), keeping category sizes roughly balanced and matching the per-category scale of OpenVE-Bench [24]. Each category covers diverse fine-grained edits, and all source videos are strictly disjoint between the training and evaluation splits. Figure 4 illustrates group sizes and examples for these categories. Metrics. Following the OpenVE-Bench protocol [24], we evaluate basic editing on OpenVE-Bench and new abilities on OpenVE++. Our automatic evaluation combines two complementary dimensions: (i) Semantic and visual alignment, using Gemini 2.5 Pro [20] and Gemini 3.8 Flash to rate instruction compliance, source consistency, and visual quality, and (ii) Temporal consistency and motion dynamics, using widely adopted VBench [30] metrics (Sec. 4.3). Together, they jointly capture editing fidelity and motion execution. We use Gemini 2.5 Pro to score edits before and after fine-tuning and to compare distillation methods, guidance scales, and training losses. Related Work Instruction-Based Video Editing. Early video editors adapt text-to-image or text-to-video prior at inference time without paired editing data, through inversion [9, 14, 52, 56, 65], attention control and sharing across frames [25, 31, 35, 36, 46, 99, 109], or feature propagation [15, 21, 85, 97, 98], and some tune the model or video representation on each source video [10, 59, 92]. Image editors also help construct paired training videos by editing source frame and using video model to generate the edited clip [2, 79, 86]. However, training data still concentrate on basic edit types such as object addition, removal, replacement, and style transfer [2, 24], while reliably changing subjects actions, expressions, or body movements remains difficult. Image Editing for Video Editing. Paired image editing data are far more abundant than paired video edits [6, 87, 103, 106, 111], and many prior works bring them to video. One group edits the first frame with an image editor and fine-tunes an image-to-video (I2V) or video diffusion model to propagate the edit, either on each source video [60] or by training added modules on videos [42, 62, 74]. Another group trains on image editing pairs by repeating frames or warping them into synthetic motion [86, 105], uses image edit pairs as in-context examples [66], or mixes image and video training in unified editors [11, 34, 55, 69, 88, 94]. third group modifies the architecture of pretrained image or video generative models, or adds adapters to them, to 2Fidelity measures similarity to the source. The IVEBench authors note that leaving edits incomplete can yield high fidelity; see their implementation discussion. 8 In contrast, I2VT enable video editing [3, 76, 96, 104]. fine-tunes an existing video editor directly on single source images along its own denoising trajectory, as in on-policy distillation [1, 19, 43, 44, 71, 114], without constructing video targets, engineering artificial motion, or altering the core architecture. 6. Conclusion We introduced I2VT, which transfers image editing capabilities to pretrained video editors using only individual source images, without paired videos or architectural changes. Across three video editors, it improves basic edits and enables new editing tasks, while outperforming offline distillation in matched comparisons. These gains carry over to whole video clips, showing that image editing supervision can improve video editing without new video training pairs.

Relation to Other Work Three lines of work are closest to I2VT: video editors trained from image pairs instead of videos, editors trained without edited targets, and on-policy distillation from image models into video models. Video Editing from Image Pairs. ViFeEdit [104] and ImVideoEdit [96] also learn video editing without video data. Both build new video editor from the text-to-video model Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B by adding spatial attention modules, keeping the pretrained 3D attention frozen, and finetuning on synthetic image-edit pairs treated as single-frame videos, with edited targets rendered in advance by an image editor. I2VT differs from them in three ways. First, instead of building new editor from text-to-video model, we keep the architecture unchanged and strengthen existing instruction-based video editors with LoRA. Second, we need no edited targets because an existing frozen image editor acts as the teacher and supervises the students own denoising rollout at every step. Third, while both works evaluate only appearance edits (style, replacement, color, addition, and removal, plus relighting and background replacement in ImVideoEdit) on their own test sets, we extend editing to action, expression, and body-movement edits. Because these edits change how subject moves across frames, they demand strong temporal consistency, and we show that the temporal quality of the edited videos stays on par with that of the base editors (Tables 8 and 9). We do not compare with ViFeEdit or ImVideoEdit directly, since ImVideoEdit released no code and ViFeEdit released code without trained weights. Editors Trained without Edited Targets. EVE [76] also trains video editor without supervised video data, building it from text-to-image model and distilling from two adapters on that model, an image-editing adapter for perframe edits and video-generation adapter for temporal consistency. In contrast, we strengthen an existing video editor without changing its architecture, using single frozen image editor and no second teacher, and temporal quality still stays on par with the base editors. BYG [81] uses no external teacher at all and trains flow-matching editors without paired examples from the frozen base models own instruction-following cues and cycle consistency, whereas our external image editor can also teach edits that the base video editor does not yet make well, such as edits that change how subject moves. UIP2P [75] and NP-Edit [41] also train editors without edited targets, though they work only on images. On-Policy Distillation from Image Models. MILD [32] improves text-to-video generation with image experts for composition, aesthetics, and text rendering. Its student rolls out whole videos, and the image experts supervise slices of the video latents along that rollout. Because its image and video models use different VAEs, MILD learns connectors to map those slices into the image latent space, anchors the transferred corrections to frozen copy of the video model, and adds an optical-flow motion reward. In contrast, I2VT rolls out single images: our video editor role-plays as an image editor and edits each source image as one-frame video, the same input the image editor receives. Since the teacher and the students share VAE latent space, we need no connectors, and training renders no multi-frame videos. A.2. Constructing Paired Video Edits Why Paired Video Edits Are Hard to Build. An editing pair needs source video and second video that differs from it only in the requested edit. Such pairs almost never occur naturally [13, 62], so existing datasets synthesize them at high cost [2] and mostly for appearance edits such as addition, removal, replacement, and style [7, 24]. Motion edits are harder still, because the target must change how subject moves while the rest of the scene, the camera, and the timing follow the source. Editing One Frame and Regenerating the Video. common shortcut edits one frame with an image editor and lets an image-to-video model generate the rest [40, 60]. These methods steer the image-to-video model with inverted source features [40] or per-video motion LoRAs [60], and where this guidance is weak, the model regenerates the motion instead of keeping the source motion. Content that is not visible in the first frame is hallucinated [7], the result drifts from the source dynamics under camera or object motion [62], and the quality of each pair is capped by the propagation model [2]. Goku [47] builds part of its Subject Movement data in this way: an image editor moves the subject in the first frame, and video model generates the clip from it. For action changes, the same video model generates both the source and the target from two text descriptions, so the source is itself synthetic, which transfers poorly to real videos [93]. Its filter discards about 88% of the generated samples, yet the released targets still do not follow the source motion (Figure S1). Asked to lower waving hand, the target lowers it and then freezes the person, and asked to turn the torso by 20 degrees, it replaces the whole dance. I2VT builds no video targets: the student learns from single images and relies on the pretrained video editor for motion. Figure S1. Released Goku Subject Movement pairs. We chose guidance 2 after rendering training frames at guidance 1, 2, and 5 with the same 50 steps (Figure S4). At guidance 1, the teacher can leave an edit undone, such as requested frown or head turn. At guidance 5, it over-edits by exaggerating expressions, removing objects the instruction does not mention, or moving the camera in background changes. Guidance 2 is compromise between these two failure modes and gives stable edits, completing all three examples in Figure S4 without these side effects. OpenVE++ OpenVE++ contains 207 clips in four groups: Action Change (73 clips with head, gaze, and arm edits), Expression Change (42), Body Movement (42), and Scene Relighting (50, with 35 light types and 10 directions, phrased differently from the training data). Overall is the mean of the four group means. The source clips come from OpenVE-3M videos that no training pool uses, so OpenVE++ follows the CC BYNC 4.0 license of OpenVE-3M. For the action, expression, and body-movement groups, VLM checks that the first frame suits the edit, and we check that the requested change does not already appear later in the clip. For relighting, Qwen3.5-27B [67] checks that the requested light would visibly change the clip, that the clip is not already lit that way, and that the light fits the scene. Finally, we check every case of the four groups by hand. Figure S5 shows edits of Bernini-R-1.3B on OpenVE++. Comparison with Other Benchmarks. Table S6 compares OpenVE++ with three recent benchmarks. Single Edit means that each instruction asks for one edit, and Open Source means that the test set is public. OpenVE++ will be released with the paper. IVEBench [12] puts motion edits, including six laughing or crying edits, into one Subject Motion Editing category and has no lighting edits. CoVEBench [91] covers expressions, actions, and lighting changes, but 583 of its 626 instructions combine several edits, so its marks in 20 Table S6 count only the 43 single-edit instructions. None of its lighting edits specifies light type and direction. GokuBench [47] has Subject Movement category without expression or lighting edits, and its test set has not been released. OpenVE++ gives each of the four task groups its own category and asks for one edit per instruction, so each group score measures one ability. H. User Study We run user study to check whether people also prefer I2VT edits over those of the base editors on OpenVE++. For each of the four task groups, we select four OpenVE++ clips and compare two pairs of editors from Table 3: Bernini-R1.3B with I2VT-1.3B, and Bernini-R-14B with I2VT-14B. Each of 20 participants judges 16 pairs of edits, two clips per task group for each editor pair. For every pair, participant chooses which edit is better overall or calls tie, without separate criteria. The participants are volunteers recruited from the authors acquaintances, and we record only their choices, with no names, contact details, or other personal data. No IRB or equivalent body reviewed the study, since it studies nothing about the participants themselves, and the participants agreed to take part without written consent form. Participants prefer I2VT over the base editor in every task group at both sizes (Table S7). I2VT-1.3B wins 68.1% of its 160 judgments and loses 6.9%. Against the stronger Bernini-R-14B, I2VT-14B wins 50.6% and loses 15.0%, and more of its judgments end in tie, most of all for body movements (50.0%). This preference agrees in direction with the Gemini 2.5 Pro scores on OpenVE++ in Table 3. I. For each edit, the Gemini judge receives the source video followed by the edited video as two video-file inputs, with category-specific scoring prompt supplied as the system instruction. We upload the complete videos without local frame extraction and leave the temperature at the API default for the Gemini 2.5 Pro runs.
